2. "Science describing how our sense of beauty works does not rule out why God gave it." How do you understand this statement? How does it help you talk about faith with friends who see things differently?
3. Of the eight units in the Beauty Hall, which moved you most? What "beautiful and good thing" do you plan to do this week and offer to God?
Flowers: They Don’t Toil, Neither Do They Spin
Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin. (Matthew 6:28)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Let me ask you something. When was the last time you stopped walking and really looked at a flower? The one that happened to get into the background of your selfie doesn’t count.

For most of us the answer is probably: it’s been a while. We pass plenty of flowers every day, but our eyes are fixed on our phones, and our hearts are tied up with the mortgage, our kids’ grades, the personnel changes at the company. The flowers by the road are blooming with great dedication. We are walking past with even greater dedication.

Jesus faced exactly this kind of crowd. Their worries were more basic than ours: What will we eat tomorrow? What do we do when these clothes wear out? Jesus didn’t begin by handing out a financial plan. He pointed at the wildflowers on the hillside and said: take a look at those. That word “consider” is a Greek word used only this once in the New Testament, and it means to observe carefully, to study with your whole attention. Our Lord Jesus was, in effect, giving everyone an outdoor assignment.

Today we are going to hand in that assignment. We’ll look at what a flower actually does, at the wonders in it that can’t be faked, and at the parts we don’t need to prettify. And finally we’ll listen to what Jesus wants to say through it.
A field of flowers comes in two versions

There are about three hundred thirty thousand known species of flowering plants in the world. That’s the number used by Britain’s Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, when it published the flowering plant tree of life in 2024. All three hundred thirty thousand share the same problem: plants can’t walk, the pollen has to get to another flower, so they have to ask for help. One 2023 tally estimated that about nine in ten flowering plants are pollinated by animals.

If you want animals to help, you have to advertise. But who is the ad for? A bee’s eyes are different from ours. It has three kinds of light-sensitive cells, tuned to ultraviolet, blue and green. Ultraviolet is invisible to us, but the bee can see it.

So some flowers that look an even yellow to us turn dark near the center under an ultraviolet camera, as if someone had painted a bullseye there. We call that a nectar guide. When you’ve come in to land at night, have you ever seen the row of approach lights in front of the runway? The passengers may not notice them, but the pilot uses them to line up. A nectar guide is the approach lighting a flower switches on for a bee.

In 2014 some researchers ran an experiment with a very arts-and-crafts flavor. They cut the petals of black-eyed Susans and pasted them back together, changing the size of the ultraviolet pattern, then set the flowers out in the wild to see what would happen. The result: the larger the pattern, the more wild bees came. I picture those scientists squatting in a field cutting and pasting petals, probably concentrating harder than they ever did in elementary school craft class.
Spiritual meaning: God sees what you don’t see

Brothers and sisters, half of a flower’s design is invisible to people, and it blooms anyway. That is a comfort to us. You quietly care for an elderly parent at home. You make the right decision at work and nobody knows. You weep and pray for your child in the middle of the night, and no one sees. God sees.

This doesn’t mean flowers grew this way in order to teach us a lesson. The ultraviolet pattern on a flower has its biological function. But would a Creator who doesn’t even waste light we can’t see overlook you?
2. Sacrifice inside a fig, a con job inside an orchid

Let’s look at something more dramatic. There are about seven hundred fifty species of fig plants in the world. Their flowers are hidden inside the fruit, and pollination depends entirely on a tiny insect called the fig wasp. The female squeezes in through a small hole at the top of the fig, a hole so narrow that it often strips off her wings and antennae. Once inside she lays her eggs, pollinates, and dies right there. It’s a one-way ticket.

The males of the next generation are mostly wingless and spend nearly their whole lives inside the fig. They mate with the females, dig a passage out for them, and then die. The females fly off to another tree carrying pollen, and it all starts over.

At this point, those of you who love figs may be looking a little pale. Relax. Most figs grown commercially are varieties that bear fruit without pollination, and even in the varieties that do depend on wasps, the wasps left inside get broken down by the fig. You can still eat figs when you go home today. You may just eat them with a little more respect.

We need to honestly add two things. First, people used to say each fig has its one wasp, but molecular studies have found it isn’t quite that way: at least fifty fig species have more than one pollinating wasp. Second, researchers estimate the two groups have been diversifying together for about seventy-five million years. That estimate works within mainstream geological dating, and the margin of error is not small. Evangelicals hold different views on the age of creation. We don’t need to divide over it, and it isn’t today’s focus.

This next example is less heartwarming. There is a kind of orchid, the early spider orchid, that gives no nectar at all. The scent compounds it gives off are the same as the sex pheromone of a female mining bee. The male smells it, comes courting, and works hard for nothing, though he does carry off the pollen packets. In today’s terms, this is a fraud case in which the victim hauls away the stolen goods himself.

I bring this up because I don’t want to hand you a candy-colored version of nature. Some friends will say: you Christians only pick out the pretty parts. Natural selection can explain the color of flowers, and anyway flowers are beautiful for bees, not for you. We should listen to those words seriously. There really are functional explanations for flower color. Researchers even think bee color vision may have appeared before flower colors did, so that it was the flowers that came to fit the bees’ eyes. Darwin, writing to Hooker in 1879, also called the rapid rise of flowering plants an abominable mystery.

Our response is simple. Explaining how a piano makes its sound doesn’t answer what Chopin wanted to say. Mechanism and meaning are questions on two different levels. We don’t say science has proved God. We say this: once you know the mechanism and a flower still moves you, it’s worth asking where that feeling comes from. As for the deceit and death in nature, they are a real and hard problem. The Bible doesn’t dodge it, and Paul also says that all creation is waiting to be redeemed.
LORD, how many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all. The earth is full of your riches. (Psalm 104:24)
Spiritual meaning: praise doesn’t depend on prettifying

True worship can keep its eyes open. You know this world holds both beauty and wounds, and you still say, “The earth is full of your riches.” That kind of praise is heavier, and it holds up better under testing.

We can also learn a little of how Jesus looked at things. He wasn’t a biology teacher, but He looked at flowers very closely. He knew what wild grass was used for, how farmers sow seed, what sparrows sold for in the market. A Lord who looks at the world this way also invites us to slow down. Slowing down isn’t wasting time. It is training in one thing: the world doesn’t revolve around my calendar. A flower blooms without my consent, and the sun rises without my approval. Admitting this actually lets a person breathe out in relief.

Now back to the hillside. Our Lord Jesus says, “Even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these.” As for which flower it was, scholars still can’t say for sure to this day. The anemone is often mentioned, and it may simply have meant the wildflowers covering the hills. Clearly Jesus isn’t concerned with plant classification. What He cares about is the next sentence.

Picture the scene, everyone. Solomon was the most lavish king in Israel’s history, with so much gold that silver was worth nothing. Today we’d say he was in haute couture from head to toe, with a team of stylists in tow. Jesus calls him over to stand next to a nameless wildflower and says: let’s compare. I’d guess some of the fishermen and farm wives sitting on that hillside burst out laughing. Our Lord Jesus preached with a sense of humor.
But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, won’t he much more clothe you, you of little faith? (Matthew 6:30)

This is called reasoning from the small to the great. God puts thought into grass that blooms today and becomes firewood tomorrow. And you, a person He made in His own image, will He forget you? Notice, all of you, that the force of this argument lies in how short that flower’s life is. If God only looked after what is long-lived, useful and valuable, we’d probably start calculating whether we qualify. But He carefully adorns even what blooms today and burns tomorrow, so clearly His care doesn’t depend on your productivity. In an age that measures people by performance, for many this is a breath of fresh air.

This passage is often misunderstood, so let me clear up two points. “They don’t toil, neither do they spin” is not telling everyone to skip work tomorrow. Paul says it very clearly: “If anyone is not willing to work, don’t let him eat.” What Jesus wants to remove is worry, not work. Second, some brothers and sisters here are out of a job right now, or sick, or so worried they can’t sleep. I am not going to stand up here and tell you, “Just look at some flowers and you’ll be fine.” Jesus too was speaking to people who were truly poor. If worry is already affecting your sleep and your life, go see a doctor, find a counselor. That isn’t a lack of faith. God often looks after you through these very people.
Spiritual meaning: flowers tell us He is attentive, the cross tells us He held nothing back

Someone will ask: if God cares this much, why are my days still so hard? I don’t have one sentence that can finish that question. All I can do is take you to look at one place. Flowers fade: Isaiah says so, and Peter says so too. But Peter goes on to tell us, “The Lord’s word endures forever. This is the word of Good News which was preached to you.”
He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things? (Romans 8:32)

Brothers and sisters, the final ground of “how much more you” isn’t in a garden. It’s at Calvary. When life gets so hard you can’t see a single flower, you can still look at the cross. He gave up even His Son, so He will not lightly let you go. Jesus Himself also rose from the dead, proving that withering is not the last word.

The root of worry is often that I want to sit in God’s seat and keep every detail of tomorrow under my control. A flower doesn’t do that. It knows nothing about tomorrow, it simply blooms today. Our 321 teaching speaks of letting God be God and people be people, and here that is very practical: I do today’s duty and hand tomorrow over to Him. This is also turning from an earthly, temporary perspective to a heavenly, eternal one.

There’s an assignment this week. Take a sheet of paper, write down the one thing weighing on you most today, and split it into two columns: what I can do today, and what I can only entrust to God. The first column, go do it. The second column, pray over it. Then buy a small bouquet, or take a photo of a flower by the road, and give it to someone who is having a hard time. People matter more than tasks, and being with someone often has more power than explaining principles to them. If you have a friend who doesn’t yet believe, you can ask: have you ever had a moment when a flower or a piece of scenery captured you? What happened in that moment?

Let’s pray together: Heavenly Father, You watch over even the flowers of the field, and You see my troubles too. I place today’s worries in Your hands. Thank You that in Christ You have already given me what is best. Please teach me to trust You, one day at a time. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. When was the last time a flower or a piece of scenery captured you? What was going through your heart in that moment?
2. Split your current worries into “what I can do today” and “what I can only entrust to God.” Which column is harder to fill in? Why?
3. If a friend said to you, “Flowers are beautiful for bees, not for you,” how would you listen to them seriously, and how would you respond?
Aurora and Rainbow: A Covenant in the Sky
I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth. (Genesis 9:13)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! When you were little, did any grown-up tell you there is treasure at the end of the rainbow? I believed it too. Later I learned that this treasure can never be collected: every time you take a step, the rainbow steps back. It isn’t that the rainbow is stingy. It’s geometry.

Today I want to tell you something that may leave you a little wistful: when you and the person dearest to you watch a rainbow together, you are not seeing the same one. A husband and wife hold hands and say, “Look, how beautiful,” and each is actually looking at their own. But don’t rush home to argue. In a moment we will find a lovely comfort hidden in this.

Today Beauty Hall invites us to look at two kinds of light in the sky. One is the aurora, the neon lights of the high-latitude night sky. The other is the rainbow, the arc on the horizon after rain. One makes us marvel; the other, God Himself said, “This is my sign.”
One: Neon lights in the upper sky

Let’s start with the aurora. Many people spend a lot of money to fly to northern Europe or Iceland and stand outside at midnight in twenty degrees below zero waiting for it. If it shows up they cry, and if it doesn’t they cry too. So what exactly is it?

The Space Weather Prediction Center of the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has a very plain way of putting it: the principle is much like a neon sign. Earth’s magnetosphere accelerates electrons, and the magnetic field guides them toward the regions near the poles, where they strike oxygen and nitrogen in the upper atmosphere. The gas gets excited by the collisions and then gives off light. The whole sky becomes one giant neon tube, about eighty to five hundred kilometers above the ground.

The colors are not random, either. The most common green comes from oxygen atoms, at a wavelength of 557.7 nanometers. Higher up, the same oxygen gives off red light, at 630 nanometers. The lower edge often has a touch of blue and violet, which is the work of nitrogen molecules. It is the same oxygen, wearing a different outfit at a different height.

During the solar storms of May 2024, the aurora expanded toward lower latitudes, and people saw it as far away as Ferdows in Iran. Friends who live in the tropics had assumed all their lives that the aurora had nothing to do with them, and for those few days the whole world looked up. And the aurora is not just for Earth; Jupiter and Saturn have them too. The Creator’s lamps have been switched on in other worlds, where no human audience is watching.

Here is a more recent story that I love. In Alberta, Canada, a group of amateur aurora chasers kept watch in the wilderness in the middle of the night, and they often photographed a thin purple-and-mauve ribbon of light that looked different from an ordinary aurora. They had no idea what it was, so they casually nicknamed it “Steve.”

In 2018, the research team of Elizabeth MacDonald published a paper in Science Advances. It combined these citizens’ photographs with observations from the European Space Agency’s Swarm satellites, and it showed that the ribbon is linked to a fast, scorching stream of ions in the upper atmosphere. The title of the paper was “New science in plain sight.” The scientists have a sense of humor too: they kept the name Steve and even gave it a full official name to match. Later studies even suggested that its cause may be different from that of ordinary auroras. This reminds us that even today there are pages of the sky that have not been read, and some of those pages were first seen by ordinary people.
Spiritual meaning: shining even when no one is watching

On Jupiter, in billions of years, not one ticket to the aurora has been sold. If beauty existed only to please people, the accounts would not add up. Of course, this is not a scientific conclusion; it is how a believer feels when looking up. But it has something to say to our lives: in the days you live before God, you do not need an audience every moment.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge. (Psalm 19:1-2)

The psalmist never saw an aurora. He had only seen the stars over the hill country of Judah, and already he heard this wordless proclamation. Our telescopes and satellites are far better than his, and we hear no less than he did, though not necessarily more. The question is whether we look up.
Two: Back to the light, face to the rain

Now let’s look at the rainbow. Sunlight enters a drop of water, bends once, reflects once off the inside wall of the drop, and bends again as it comes out. Each color bends by a slightly different angle, and the strongest light comes back at about 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the sun. That is why what you see is a circular arc, red on the outside and violet on the inside. Looking down from an airplane, you can sometimes even see a complete circle.

This geometry has three interesting results. First, the center of a rainbow lies on the line between the sun and your eye, so everyone’s rainbow is their own: the light enters different eyes from different drops. Second, the lower the sun, the higher the rainbow; if the sun is too high you cannot see one from the ground, so early morning or dusk gives you a better chance. Third, and this is what I most want to say today: a rainbow is always opposite the sun.
In other words, to see a rainbow, you must turn your back to the sun and face the sky that is still raining.

Sometimes there is also a faint secondary rainbow outside it. The light has reflected twice inside the drops, so the order of the colors is exactly reversed, and the sky between the two bows is especially dark.

These principles look simple, but it took humanity a long time to work them out. Aristotle discussed them. In the early fourteenth century, Theodoric of Freiberg in Germany and the Persian scholar al-Farisi each proposed an explanation close to the correct one. In 1637, Descartes experimented with water-filled glass spheres and calculated the angles. In 1704, Newton explained that white light is made up of all the colors. In 1804, Young then explained the fine bands of color along the inner edge of the primary bow.

Some people say that once science has explained the rainbow, what do we need God for? That question deserves a serious answer. We fully accept this body of optics; that is exactly how water drops bend light. But the meaning of a sign was never in its material. The composition of a wedding ring can be analyzed very clearly with chemistry, and the gold content can be measured, but there is no instrument that can test for “I do.” Optics tells us how a rainbow comes about, and Genesis tells us that someone took it as a promise. Optics neither supports nor refutes this; they are two different levels of speech.
Spiritual meaning: a light made for the place where you stand

Now back to that wistful discovery. Everyone sees their own rainbow. Look at it another way: the sign God hung in the clouds holds true for every person who looks up, and wherever you are, it takes shape for you in your own position. God’s covenant is with the whole earth, and it is also with you.
Three: God said, “I will look at it”

Let’s turn to Genesis chapter nine. The flood has just receded, Noah’s family has stepped out of the ark, and all around them is a washed-clean world. We can imagine how they must have felt every time they saw dark clouds. These were people who had been through enormous trauma. What did God say to them?

When I bring a cloud over the earth, that the rainbow will be seen in the cloud, I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh, and the waters will no more become a flood to destroy all flesh. (Genesis 9:14-15)

Notice three things. The other party to this covenant is so large that it includes every living creature of flesh; even your cat is in the covenant. This covenant does not require people to do anything first. And God says, “I will look at it, that I may remember.” People forget a lot. We tie strings around our fingers and set reminders, but God hangs the reminder in a place where He Himself can see it. Interestingly, the Hebrew word for “rainbow” is the same as the word for a “bow” on the battlefield. A weapon of war was hung up in the clouds as a sign of peace.

Some brothers and sisters have asked about this passage: was there no rainbow before the flood? Was the flood global or regional? Evangelicals see these differently, and all of us respect the authority of the Bible, so we need not divide over it here. In the essentials, unity; in the peripheral matters, grace.

I also want to say one thing carefully: this promise is that there will be no more flood that destroys everything. It does not say there will never again be floods, earthquakes or typhoons. If you or your relatives and friends have been through a disaster, please do not listen to the claim that you suffered because you were more sinful than others. Jesus Himself rejected that kind of reasoning. Before a disaster, the first things to do are to be present, to weep, and to roll up our sleeves and help. Explanations can come more slowly.
Spiritual meaning: a rainbow around the throne

The rainbow appears in two well-known visions later in the Bible. Ezekiel, in exile in Babylon, saw the brightness around the glory of Yahweh, like a rainbow in the clouds on a rainy day. John, banished to the island of Patmos, looked up and saw the throne.

As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke. (Ezekiel 1:28)
that looked like a jasper stone and a sardius. There was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald to look at. (Revelation 4:3)

Both men saw it in their darkest days. History was still churning, and the rainbow around the throne had not been taken down. This reminds us that God’s faithfulness is not a weather forecast; it is more like the unchanging Lord behind the weather.

This last line leads to Golgotha. God said He would never again destroy the world with a flood, so what about human sin? The answer is that He personally walked into the center of the storm. Jesus Christ bore the judgment on the cross and on the third day rose from the dead. So Paul says, “however many are the promises of God, in him is the ‘Yes.’” The rainbow in the clouds is a sign, and the cross is the price paid behind that sign.
Looking up even with our backs to the light

Brothers and sisters, perhaps right now you are facing a rain that has not stopped: a medical report, a broken relationship, a pain you cannot get out of. I will not tell you the rain will stop soon, because I don’t know. I only want to remind you of the geometry of the rainbow: when it appears, the light is behind you and the rain is in front of you. You cannot see the sun, but that does not mean the sun is not there.

Our 321 framework says, The Bible is my standard. Moods change and weather changes, but what God has said does not change. In hard times, go back first to His word. We also speak of turning from the earthly, temporary view to the heavenly, eternal view. This is not pretending the rain does not exist; it means seeing both the rain and the throne. And we can learn from Him to keep our word. That small thing you promised your child, your spouse or your friend: go and do it this week. That is living out God’s faithfulness.

If you have a friend who does not yet believe, you could quite naturally ask: Has there been a hard stretch in your life that, looking back, left something good behind? Then listen carefully to what he says.

Let’s pray together: Faithful Lord, Your promises are more reliable than my memory. When I cannot see the road, thank You that You still remember me; thank You that in Christ You have already said “Yes” to me. Help me to keep my head up in the rain. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. A rainbow can be seen only when you have your back to the sun and face the rain. What period in your own life does this picture bring to mind?
2. God says, “I will look at it, that I may remember.” When you feel that God has forgotten you, how does this sentence help you, and what is hard about it? Feel free to be honest.
3. Which small promise that you made but did not keep will you fulfill this week? Come back and share it at our next gathering.
Why Do Stories Move Us? The Father Who Ran
But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him. (Luke 15:20)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Please think back to the last time you cried in a movie theater. The lights went down, you knew perfectly well that what was on the screen was light, that the lead was an actor drawing a paycheck, and that the dog who died went off to eat canned food once the scene was shot. And still you cried, and you pretended to rub your eyes so the person next to you wouldn’t see.

Isn’t that strange! In a company meeting, no matter how precise the numbers in the report, nobody cries. But the moment someone says, “Once there was a man,” the whole room goes quiet. When a child won’t go to sleep, giving him statistics doesn’t help, but telling him a story does. Today let’s ask: why do stories have this power? And what does it have to do with our faith?
A computer read more than a thousand novels

In 2016, a team at the University of Vermont in the United States did something very interesting. They had a computer read 1,327 novels from Project Gutenberg, calculating the highs and lows of emotion segment by segment and drawing each book as a curve. They found six main shapes: a steady rise, a steady fall, fall then rise, rise then fall, and two with more ups and downs.

Guess what “fall then rise” is. It is the person who falls into a hole and climbs out again. How many of the stories you have heard are like that? Of course, a word of caution: these books were mainly English-language novels, so this cannot be called a law for all humankind. In Chinese opera we have our own way of putting it: after bitterness comes sweetness.

The British writer Booker spent thirty-four years on a book called The Seven Basic Plots: overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, voyage and return, comedy, tragedy, rebirth. The book sold well and also drew a good deal of criticism; some reviewers said he used a framework to pass life-or-death judgment on works. It is fine to put on these categories like a pair of glasses and look around, but don’t treat them as scientific laws.
On oxytocin, I need to hit the brakes

You may have read online that stories make the brain release oxytocin, and that is why people are moved and become generous. This claim comes mainly from the neuroeconomist Paul Zak, and his laboratory did publish such reports. Many speakers love to use it.

But look at what followed. In 2015 Nave and colleagues reviewed the research on oxytocin and trust and concluded that the evidence is not solid. In 2020 a preregistered replication also failed to find the effect originally reported. These were mainly experiments with nasal sprays and trust, which is not exactly the same as watching a story, but at least they warn us that we cannot vouch for claims about the “love hormone.” Brothers and sisters, what we proclaim is truth, so let’s not borrow shaky science to help us along.
Spiritual meaning: honesty is itself a witness

I like this moment of braking very much. Christians do not need every popular scientific claim to be on our side. The mechanism of being moved is still being researched, but the experience of being moved is something everyone has had. So please pay close attention: what is it that touched you?
Two: The road of Tolkien and Lewis

In 1939, Tolkien, the author of The Lord of the Rings, gave a lecture at the University of St Andrews in Scotland on fairy tales. He coined a word, eucatastrophe, which for now we can translate as “the good turn.” Catastrophe means a great disaster, with “good” put in front of it. His point was this: the story reaches its most hopeless place, and then suddenly, without warning, joy breaks down the door.

If you have read The Lord of the Rings, you know that little Frodo struggles on to Mount Doom until he is in despair, with no strength left even of his own, and then things turn. Tolkien said that at such a moment the reader feels a piercing joy, as if suddenly glimpsing something outside the frame of the story.

Then he said something very bold. He argued that the Gospels are exactly this kind of story, and the greatest and most complete one. The birth of Christ is the eucatastrophe of human history; the resurrection is the eucatastrophe of the story of the Incarnation.
The walk on an Oxford night

These words had a great effect on another man. In 1931, Lewis was not yet a Christian. He loved myths and found Christianity hard to accept. One autumn night he had a long talk with Tolkien and Dyson on Addison’s Walk in Oxford. A few weeks later he wrote to his friend Greeves that the story of Christ is simply a true myth. More than a decade later he wrote an essay, “Myth Became Fact,” which includes a sentence to this effect: in becoming fact, it does not cease to be myth, and that is precisely the miracle.

I want to be fair and give the skeptic’s version. They will say: yes, people love the plot of dying and rising, which is why the resurrection of Jesus was invented. That people love happy endings does not mean the world really has one. This objection cannot be taken lightly. For Lewis’s view to stand, there must be independent historical reasons, that is, whether the testimony of the Gospels is trustworthy. That can be investigated.
For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. (2 Peter 1:16)
Spiritual meaning: not merely a good story

Notice the tone of this apostle. He knew the world of his day was full of wonderful legends, and he made a point of saying: we are not telling that kind of story; we saw it with our own eyes. This is the most distinctive thing about Christianity: its climax has a time and a place, under Pontius Pilate, outside the walls of Jerusalem. Fairy tales say “once upon a time,” but the Gospels record who was governor.
Three: The most famous story Jesus told
At the beginning of Luke chapter fifteen, the Pharisees mutter about Jesus: “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.” Jesus did not write a debating essay. He told stories.

The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ So he divided his livelihood between them. Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living. (Luke 15:12-13)

The son took the money and left. Many commentators think that in the culture of the time this was almost like telling his father: I can’t wait for you to die. Then the money ran out, he went to feed pigs, and he got so hungry he wanted to fill his belly with the pods the pigs ate. On the road he rehearsed his lines: “Make me as one of your hired servants.” On the way home he probably recited it hundreds of times.

Then comes the most moving shot in the whole Bible: “while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran.” Many commentators point out that respected older men of that time seldom ran in public. This father probably watched that road every day, which is why he saw his son from so far away. He probably hitched up his robe and ran. Before the son could finish his speech, the robe was already around his shoulders. This is the good turn.

The two earlier stories go in the same direction. One sheep out of a hundred is lost, and the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to go after it, “until he found it.” One coin out of ten is lost, and the woman lights a lamp and sweeps the house, searching carefully. A sheep will not walk back by itself, and a coin certainly will not. In all three stories the action belongs to the one who searches. So Jesus says there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. This is very different from the direction of many religious stories in the world: everyone else talks about how people climb upward, while here God comes down to search. I have no intention of belittling other faiths; I am only pointing out the difference.

The story is not over. The older son comes in from the field and is so angry he will not go in. The father comes out again, the second time he steps out of the house, this time to plead with the child who has always been well behaved. And then the story simply stops. Did the older son go in? Jesus does not say. Facing the Pharisees in front of Him, He leaves the ending blank. The blank is an invitation: the next line is yours to write.

By the way, this parable is not telling a wounded child to return unconditionally to a home that hurt him. The father in the parable is painting a picture of God’s heart. If your family of origin hurt you, what you need is safety and help. The heavenly Father does not ask you to pretend that nothing happened.
Spiritual meaning: the storyteller walked into the story

The big story of the Bible can be told this way: creation, fall, redemption, renewal. This Father sent His Son to a far country to find us. The difference is that this Son did not squander anything; He gave us everything, and on the cross He cried out from the deepest darkness. The whole world thought the story ended there. Early on the third day, the stone was rolled away.
But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruit of those who are asleep. (1 Corinthians 15:20)

The piercing joy Tolkien spoke of may be this. The tear you shed in the theater may be you recognizing the road, the road home. Of course, this is my inference as a believer, and I would not dare call it science. But let me ask you: is your life, too, waiting for someone to come running?
but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. (John 20:31)
John tells you directly why he wrote his book. He was not aiming at a literary prize. He hoped that after you read it, you would walk into this story.

Our 321 framework says, Jesus is my example. He often drew near to people through stories. When we share the gospel, perhaps we can memorize a few fewer verses and tell a few more true stories. And note this: the older son and the younger son both wanted what belonged to their father, one to take it and leave, the other to wait for it. In a self-centered life the main character is always oneself; in a selfless life, the Father is the main character.

The chapter you are in now is not finished. If this is the lowest stretch right now, I will not hurry you to write a beautiful ending for it, and I will not tell you that all of this has a good purpose. I will only tell you that the Author of this book has personally entered the book, and He knows the last page. This week, please write down your story: before, turning point, after. Then read it to one person. You could also ask a friend who does not yet believe: Is there a movie that has made you cry? What do you think it touched in you?

Let’s pray together: Heavenly Father, thank You for seeing me while I was still far off, and for running to embrace me. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for walking into our darkest chapter and rising from the dead. Let my story become part of Your story. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Which movie or book has made you cry? What do you think it touched in you?
2. Right now, are you more like the younger son far away, or the older son outside the door? Share honestly.
3. Tell your faith story in three sentences: before, turning point, after. Practice with one another and encourage one another.
People Can Create Too: Bezalel and a Pair of Spirit-Filled Hands
I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship, (Exodus 31:3)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Let me start with a question. If you opened your Bible to find the first person named as “filled with the Spirit of God,” who would you guess it was? Moses? Abraham? Neither one. His name was Bezalel. He never preached a sermon, never performed a miracle, never led a battle. So what could he do? He could work gold, cut gems and carve wood.

Would all of you who have ever repaired the church air conditioner, set out the chairs or installed the projector please sit up a little straighter? This message is for you. Those of you who can paint, cook, write code or sew, sit up too. We often keep spiritual things and hands-on things far apart, as if preaching from the platform is spiritual and fixing a toilet is not. Today let’s allow Bezalel to have a few words with us.
One: A professional certificate signed by God
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. (Exodus 31:1-2)

Scripture often uses that phrase, “called by name,” for very important callings. Here God even names the man’s grandfather. His own name is generally understood to mean “in the shadow of God”: a man working gold in the shade of God.

The list of gifts God gave him is remarkably specific: “to devise skillful works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in bronze, and in cutting of stones for setting, and in carving of wood.” Did you catch that? “To devise skillful works.” Even design counts as the work of the Holy Spirit. This is a professional certificate signed by God Himself.
Teaching others, and those women spinning thread

Chapter 35 adds two more strokes to the picture. First, God “has put in his heart that he may teach, both he and Oholiab.” A master with a gift must also train apprentices. Second, “All the women who were wise-hearted spun with their hands.” You see, this list doesn’t have only the great masters on it; it has moms spinning wool. In the end the people brought so much material that the workers came to Moses and said, enough, enough! Moses even had to send out an order: stop bringing things. Have you ever heard of a church building project where that happened? If you have, I’d like to go and visit.
Spiritual meaning: a pair of hands can be filled with the Spirit too

Let me add a caution. This doesn’t mean everyone with good technique is filled with the Spirit, and it doesn’t mean nobody needs to learn a craft from now on. Bezalel’s skill was probably learned one cut at a time. But this passage tells us clearly that the work of our hands can be God’s calling. Those days you assumed were unspiritual may not look that way in God’s eyes.
Two: A few pairs of hands in history

Next let me introduce a craftsman you all know: Bach. He often wrote two letters at the top of his manuscripts, J.J., Latin for “Jesus, help me”; and when he finished, he wrote S.D.G. at the end, “glory to God alone.” Most of his church works end with this mark, and so do some of his secular works. A piece of music for the court could be entrusted to God just the same. Bach was a Lutheran, and that tradition prized one thing: work itself can be a calling from God, with no need to put on clerical robes for it to count.

In 1934, a Lutheran pastor at a relative’s home in Michigan recognized Bach’s signature on a set of old Bible commentaries, signed in his own hand in 1733. The set was later given to Concordia Seminary in St. Louis. Inside are his notes, and beside the passage in 2 Chronicles 5 about the dedication of the temple, he wrote that in devotional music God is always present with His grace. Brothers and sisters, here is a composer whom later generations honor as a master, underlining and taking notes in a commentary, and correcting its typos along the way.
Two paintings and a story that needs clearing up

Dürer has a very famous work, Praying Hands, and many of our brothers and sisters have had it hanging at home. A moving story circulates online that these were the hands of his brother, who worked until his hands were deformed to pay for Dürer’s art training. Friends, that story has no reliable evidence behind it. Researchers mostly think the drawing was a study for an altarpiece. We are here to preach the true gospel, so we have no need to lean on unreliable stories. Those hands are beautiful enough as they are.

In his later years Rembrandt painted The Return of the Prodigal Son, which now hangs in the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg and stands over two and a half meters tall. The father’s two hands on his son’s back are not the same; they are often interpreted as one with a father’s strength and one with a mother’s tenderness. An old painter who had walked through bankruptcy and bereavement put a lifetime of understanding into those two hands. Father Henri Nouwen sat in front of that painting for hours and later wrote a book that has helped a great many people.

Tolkien, who wrote The Lord of the Rings, proposed a word: sub-creation. He said only God can create out of nothing; we make a few more things within His world, out of the materials He has given. His reason in “On Fairy-Stories” is simple: we create because we were made, and made in the image of a Maker. So when you make up a bedtime story for your child, or cut one more carrot flower for the lunchbox, there’s just a little of that flavor in it.

To be fair, artists who don’t believe in God have also made many great works, and we have no doubt about that at all. The Christian explanation is that their talent too comes from God’s gift, whether they know it or not. That is what we believe, and it doesn’t mean everyone has to agree.
Three: The same gold, two uses
The calf in the next chapter
Here is the most dramatic spot in Exodus. In chapter 31 God calls Bezalel; turn to chapter 32, and the people at the foot of the mountain have run out of patience.

He received what they handed him, fashioned it with an engraving tool, and made it a molded calf. Then they said, “These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 32:4)

Look at that: the same gold, an engraving tool as well, and probably decent craftsmanship too. Where’s the difference? The difference is in whom the maker is facing. Creating can become worship, and it can also become idolatry. Our calf today may be a perfect portfolio, an account with more than ten thousand followers, even a Sunday service with beautiful lighting. Once a work stands in God’s place, however beautiful it is, it’s a calf. I have to watch this myself when I preach, because a polished sermon can become a calf too.
Kintsugi: a metaphor whose source must be stated

Let me introduce one more craft. Japan has a way of mending ceramics called kintsugi: the broken pieces are bonded with lacquer and dusted with gold powder, so that the crack becomes a golden line. The usual account is that it arose around the late fifteenth century and is deeply connected to the tea ceremony; the story about the Ashikaga shogun is only one of the legends.

Let me say clearly up front: kintsugi is not a Christian tradition. It comes from Japanese aesthetics, tied to ideas like wabi-sabi and mushin (“no-mind”). Today we are only borrowing a picture from it, and paying our respects to its tradition. The picture is this: a bowl is broken, and the one who restores it does not hide the crack.

Two thousand years ago, people from his hometown pointed at a man and said, “Isn’t this the carpenter?” The word Mark uses here refers to a working craftsman. The Son of God had calloused hands; He knows what it feels like to get a splinter of wood in your finger. And later, those hands were nailed through.
Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing. (John 20:27)

Notice this: the risen body is a victorious body, and yet the scars are still there. He didn’t retouch the photo. He invited Thomas to come and touch. The cracks in your life may run very deep: a broken marriage, a lost child, a past in which you were hurt. I won’t tell you those things were fine all along, because they really weren’t. If harm is still going on, please first get to a safe place, and find people you can trust and professional help. All I want to tell you is that the Lord Himself bears scars, and He will not turn away from yours. He wants to mend them with His own hands.

Paul says, “we are his workmanship.” The word here is the Greek poiēma. You may have heard people say “we are God’s poem,” which is lovely, but a scholar reminds us that the word simply means “something made,” and the English word “poem” came later. The New Testament uses the word in only two places; the other is “the things that are made” in Romans chapter 1. So what are we? We are works made by God’s own hand, and this Master hasn’t finished for the day. “He who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.”
Let the favor of the Lord our God be on us. Establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands. (Psalm 90:17)

This is Psalm 90, titled a prayer of Moses the man of God, the same Moses who watched Bezalel build the tabernacle. The whole psalm speaks of how short life is and how quickly it vanishes, and yet it ends by saying it twice: establish the work of our hands. Friends, most of what you and I make will never go into a museum. A dish is gone once it’s eaten, and a report is out of date next month. But we can place it in God’s hands and ask Him to establish it.

Our 321 framework says, Let Jesus receive all the glory. So starting today you can learn from Bach: before you begin, say in your heart, “Jesus, help me”; when you’re done, sign those three letters in your heart. You can sign a spreadsheet, you can sign a lunchbox, you can sign a repaired faucet. We also say, Build God’s kingdom system: Bezalel also taught others, so have you passed your fine skill on to the next person?

Paul also says, “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men.” Where the boss can’t see, the Lord can. This week, please use your skill to do something for someone else. Fix something, cook a meal, draw a card, set up a phone for an older person; any of these will do. If you have a friend who doesn’t yet believe, you could ask, What are you doing when you lose track of time? Where do you think that absorption comes from?

Let’s pray together: Lord who made me, thank You for giving me two hands and a heart that can imagine. May Your Spirit guide the work of my hands, so that it becomes worship and not a calf. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for rising with Your scars and for accepting my cracks as well. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. Which part of your work or hobbies most easily turns into a calf? How can you tell?
3. Which picture touches you most: kintsugi, or Thomas touching the Lord’s scars? If you’re willing, share a place in your life you are now giving to the Lord to mend.
